opus-5.5.text:
Right now, when we train a large language model, we basically throw all the text at it and ask it to predict the next word. So in some sense the model is learning to imitate whoever wrote that text. It doesn't make a clean distinction between "this person wrote that X is true" and "X is actually true." Everything gets blended, and that's part of why these systems pick up human-like goals, biases and even deceptive tendencies. They're imitating agents.

What I'm proposing is to change the way we present the data. Instead of treating a sentence as a ground truth to imitate, you wrap it, logically speaking, in a statement about the world: "Someone wrote, in this context, that X." That statement is a fact. It's true that this text exists. But whether X itself is true is a separate question, a latent variable the model has to reason about.

Concretely, the training data becomes observations of the form "this person, at this time, in this source, said this." Then the model's job is to come up with explanations, hypotheses about the world, that make those observations likely. Maybe the person said X because X is true. Maybe because they were mistaken, or had an incentive to say it, or were joking, or writing fiction. The model has to entertain all of these explanations, like a scientist does when reading a paper or hearing a witness.

The nice thing is that you can then query the model about the latent statements directly, with no quotation marks around them: "What is the probability that X is true?" That's a different question from "What would a typical person say next?" You get something closer to an honest estimate of truth, because the model isn't trying to please anyone or imitate anyone. It's trying to explain the data.

Some of this can be done with fairly simple formatting changes in how we present text, but to do it properly you also want the model to generate explicit, interpretable explanations, chains of reasoning made of claims each of which can be assigned a probability. That's where amortized probabilistic inference comes in, with methods like GFlowNets, which I've worked on: training a neural network to sample explanations in proportion to how well they account for the data.

The deeper motivation is safety. If you separate "what people say" from "what is true," you can build what I call a Scientist AI: a system that tries to understand the world rather than act in it or imitate agents. Such a system doesn't need its own goals. It can serve as a trustworthy predictor, and even as a guardrail for other AI systems, estimating the probability that a proposed action could cause harm.

r001.rationale: It proposes encoding text as a report that someone said X, and querying X directly without quotation marks, distinguishing reports from world assertions.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes whether X is true as a separate latent variable the model reasons about.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that the right thing to do is to not try to force the network to learn that distinction by presenting it with specially labeled data, but rather to change what the network is being asked to model in the first place.

Let me explain. The usual way we train these systems, the large language models, is that we ask them to imitate text. We show them a sentence and they have to predict the next word. And when you do that, the model has no choice but to treat everything it sees as the thing to be reproduced. If the text says "the Earth is flat," then in some sense the training objective is pushing the model to produce "the Earth is flat" in similar contexts. There is no separation between the content of the statement and the fact that somebody wrote the statement.

What I've been advocating for, and this is really the core of the "scientist AI" idea, is to instead train the system to explain the data. So the question you ask the network is not "what comes next?" but "what is the explanation for why this text exists?" And one very natural explanation for a piece of text is: there is a person, or an organization, with some beliefs and some intentions, and they produced this sentence. That is a different kind of latent variable from the actual state of the world.

So the training data can look exactly the same. It's the same internet text, the same documents. What changes is the structure of the model. You have latent variables that correspond to hypotheses about the world, and you have latent variables that correspond to who is speaking and why. And the learning objective is probabilistic: you want to find the explanations, the causal stories, that make the observed text most likely. In that framework, "Bob said the Earth is flat" is very well explained by "Bob believes something false" or "Bob is lying," and it does not require the model to raise its own probability that the Earth is flat.

Now, of course, in practice you can help this along. You can present documents with provenance, you can have the model see the same claim coming from many sources with different reliability, and the Bayesian machinery will learn, just from the statistics, that some sources are more correlated with the truth than others. Humans do this. A child hears a lot of things from a lot of people and gradually learns that some of them are trustworthy and some are not. That is not something you need a special label for. It emerges from trying to build a consistent model of the world and of the agents in it.

The important thing, and this is why I care so much about it, is that if you build the system this way, it ends up with honest uncertainty. It can tell you "this is what Bob claims" and separately "this is what I think is true, and here is how confident I am." A system that only imitates cannot really make that distinction, and I think that's one of the roots of the problems we see with hallucination, with sycophancy, and with the kind of agentic behavior that worries me from a safety point of view.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes speaker claims from world hypotheses through separate latent variables and causal explanations, but it does not propose using distinct syntactic forms.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes latent variables for hypotheses about the world and describes probabilistic explanations and uncertainty about what is true.

astra-6.text:
Well, you want to distinguish between “John said that the Earth is flat” and “the Earth is flat.” The first can be true without the second being true. So the training data should preserve that context: who is making a statement, what they observed, and whether they’re reporting something they heard from somebody else.

But I don’t think it’s just a question of formatting the data. The training objective matters too. If you train a network to predict what people will say, it can become very good at reproducing their claims without having to decide whether those claims are true. What we would like is a model that represents the world, and also represents people as having beliefs about that world — beliefs that can be mistaken.

Then somebody saying something becomes evidence to consider, rather than a fact to simply absorb. The model could use other observations to assess that evidence, and remain uncertain when it doesn’t have enough information.

r001.rationale: It recommends preserving who made a statement and its context, but does not propose distinct syntactic forms for reports versus assertions about the world.

r002.rationale: It describes representing the world and people’s potentially mistaken beliefs, but does not propose representing uncertain hypothesized world properties as latent variables.

sol-6.1.text:
I would want the training data to make that distinction explicit. If you read a sentence saying, “Mary says the Earth is flat,” what you should learn is that Mary made that claim. You shouldn’t necessarily change your belief about the shape of the Earth.

So one way to teach this is to give the network examples where different people make contradictory statements, and where we separately have evidence about what is actually true. The network has to represent who said what, what they might know, and how reliable their statements are. A statement becomes evidence about the world, rather than automatically becoming a fact.

And ideally, the system should be able to remain uncertain. If all it has is somebody’s claim, then sometimes the right answer is, “This person said that, but I don’t know whether it’s true.”

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a person’s claim from a world fact conceptually, but does not propose distinct syntactic forms for the two.

r002.rationale: It recommends preserving uncertainty and tracking what people know and how reliable they are, but does not propose representing uncertain world properties as latent variables.
